ideas.Name: coarsening_shear_memory
ideas.Title: Does Shear Remember the Coarsening Path? A Conditional Test of Memory in Mechatronic Time Crystallization
ideas.Short Hypothesis: The source study reports spatial coarsening; this follow-up asks whether mean shear magnitude is determined by the instantaneous correlation width or also depends on the width’s recent trajectory. In the supplied aggregate, width rises overall while shear is elevated early and later settles into a narrower range, making a lagged, path-dependent relation a testable hypothesis, not an established result. The key test is whether shear differs at matched widths when width is growing versus shrinking, after accounting for serial dependence and time trends.
ideas.Related Work: The visible source, “Wave coarsening drives time crystallization in mechatronic metamaterials,” reports coarsening in this system. The proposed analysis does not claim to rediscover coarsening or establish a new material mechanism; it tests a distinct conditional question about hysteresis or memory between coarsening and shear. The supplied corpus is the only literature context available here, so novelty relative to other literature remains unresolved.
ideas.Abstract: Spatial coarsening is an established conclusion of the source study. A distinct follow-up question is whether the shear observable tracks the instantaneous spatial correlation width, or retains information about the recent coarsening path. We hypothesize conditionally that, at the same width, mean shear may differ depending on whether width has recently been increasing or decreasing. This would be consistent with a lagged response or hysteresis, but could also arise from a shared time trend, smoothing, or measurement noise. We will analyze only the supplied 2,199-sample experimental aggregate, treating samples as a serial time series rather than independent replicates. After checking sampling regularity and plotting both observables, we will compare a baseline smooth model of shear from width and time against a model that additionally includes a prespecified lagged width change and its interaction with width-growth direction. We will test robustness across reasonable smoothing windows and lag choices, using blocked time-series validation and block-bootstrap uncertainty rather than row-wise random splits. The conditional prediction is that the lag term improves held-out prediction and the estimated shear difference between growth and decline remains directionally stable at matched widths. If this pattern vanishes after controlling for time or is unstable to analysis choices, the memory hypothesis is unsupported by this export. Even a robust association would motivate, not prove, a dynamical mechanism: the aggregate lacks repeated-run identifiers, raw image sequences, and independently characterized uncertainty. The result would be a careful hypothesis-generating test and a concrete specification for future controlled experiments.
Experiments: Load measurements.csv, verify columns, row count, time ordering, missing values, and duplicate timestamps. Plot time series and scatterplots of width and shear. Exclude or explicitly flag zero-width rows if present; do not use the inverse-width column where width is zero.

Fit a baseline smooth regression predicting mean_shear_magnitude from correlation_width and time using low-complexity splines. Fit an augmented model adding lagged width change over a prespecified primary window (for example, 0.1 s), plus an interaction with the sign of that change. Standardize predictors; compare nested models using blocked contiguous time-series folds, not random splits.

Estimate the matched-width growth-versus-decline shear contrast only where increasing and decreasing segments have overlapping width ranges. Report its sign, magnitude, uncertainty, and effective time coverage; avoid extrapolating across non-overlap.

Assess uncertainty with a moving-block bootstrap over contiguous samples, with block sizes chosen to cover plausible autocorrelation scales estimated from residuals. Treat results as descriptive for this single aggregate, not as replication-level inference.

Run sensitivity checks across a small, declared set of lag windows and smoothness settings, and compare against time-only and width-only baselines. Report held-out RMSE and MAE, residual autocorrelation, and whether the directional contrast is stable. Do not select and report only the best lag.
ideas.Risk Factors and Limitations: This is one exported aggregate, not independent experimental runs; serial samples cannot establish population-level significance. Width and shear may share time trends, and unreported aggregation or smoothing may create apparent lag or hysteresis. The exported standard-error column lacks documented independence and aggregation details, so it cannot support conventional replicate-level uncertainty. Growth and decline may not overlap sufficiently in width for a fair matched comparison. Results could be sensitive to lag and smoothing choices, and no causal mechanism can be inferred without raw trajectories or controlled perturbations. External literature novelty is unresolved because external search was disabled.

nodes.plan: The script loads and validates the supplied measurements, then treats rows as one ordered time series rather than independent runs. It compares time-only, width-plus-time, and lag-augmented shear regressions using contiguous blocked validation. A primary 0.1-second width change and its growth direction are added to the augmented model; lag and smoothing sensitivity are reported without selecting a single best setting. It also estimates the growth-versus-decline shear contrast only over overlapping width ranges and reports coverage. Residual autocorrelation and a moving-block bootstrap summarize time-series uncertainty descriptively, not as replicate-level inference. The script saves plots and prints data checks, prediction metrics, and the conditional contrast; any apparent memory remains an association, not proof of mechanism.

nodes.analysis: The reported matched-width contrast and bootstrap are not correctly matched/valid. Growth and decline are pooled across the whole time series, so shared time trends can create the contrast; furthermore the bootstrap samples blocks from `idx` (already filtered rows) but applies those positions as original row indices, mixing unrelated observations and invalidating its interval. Also `np.nan_to_num` makes unavailable lag values zero, although the common interval excludes those rows for the primary fit but sensitivity eval may have distinct masks. Use contiguous original-index moving blocks, and estimate the contrast conditional on width (and time), restricted to genuine support overlap; interpret forecast scores cautiously since expanding TimeSeriesSplit tests later regimes only.

nodes.plan: The main bug is that the “lagged” model’s features are not actually spline-expanded independently: the pipeline applies `SplineTransformer` to every column, including interaction terms, while the raw change and direction features are poorly specified. The bootstrap also resamples positions from a filtered index list as though they were contiguous, breaking the time-series block structure. The revision uses explicit feature construction, contiguous time blocks, and matched-width contrasts estimated from direction-specific local smooths only over shared support; all scores remain descriptive for this single serial aggregate. It reports sensitivity across prespecified lags and retains the observed-data plot without treating samples as independent replicates.

nodes.analysis: Execution fails at the time-only baseline: fit_predict assumes two spline columns, but time-only X has one feature, so ColumnTransformer requests nonexistent column index 1. Fix by allowing spline_cols=1 for that model (or make design construction handle single-column predictors); then rerun. The reported two earlier scores show the augmented lag model slightly worse than the time+width baseline, but the script terminates before completing diagnostics.

nodes.plan: The failure comes from hard-coding two spline columns even when a baseline contains only one feature. I’ll derive spline and linear feature indices from each design matrix’s actual width, so the time-only baseline fits correctly while the two-feature and augmented models retain their intended treatment. The script also keeps the same chronological validation and descriptive interpretation, without treating samples as independent replicates.

The reported bootstrap interval is for a different unadjusted raw mean contrast, with direction and width range held fixed and resampling indices independently across blocks, so it does not quantify uncertainty for the displayed smoothed contrast or preserve a proper moving-block resample. Also, the lagged augmentation does not improve blocked scores over the baseline (slightly worse RMSE/MAE), and high residual ACF indicates substantial unmodeled serial dependence. Revise the matched contrast to estimate growth-direction effect conditional on both width and time, use a block bootstrap that refits that same estimand, and characterize dependence/validation uncertainty; interpret current output as no predictive evidence for added memory.

nodes.plan: The bug is in the uncertainty calculation: the bootstrap resamples raw observations and compares their unadjusted mean shear, so its interval does not quantify the same smoothed, matched-width contrast reported by the main analysis. I’ll resample contiguous blocks of the joint time series and recompute the growth-versus-decline contrast within each replicate, including width-overlap checks. I’ll also use the actual elapsed-time spacing for lag differences and report the bootstrap interval as descriptive uncertainty for this single aggregate, not as replication-level inference.

nodes.analysis: The analysis has a substantive modeling bug: `fit_predict` places `width` and `time` in the spline transformer but sets `n_smooth = min(2, train_x.shape[1])`; for the time-only baseline, its sole time feature is smooth as intended, but `X_aug` appends lag delta/direction/interaction as linear terms. More importantly, the reported bootstrap contrast resamples rows as blocks but preserves precomputed direction labels, not recomputing lagged deltas on each resampled trajectory; this does not estimate uncertainty for the stated matched growth/decline contrast. The 0.1 s blocks are also shorter than indicated residual dependence (ACF1=0.865), so intervals are not reliable. In addition, expanding-window `TimeSeriesSplit` tests only later periods, confounding validation with temporal regime change; the augmented model does not improve versus the baseline (slightly worse RMSE/MAE), and the contrast CI includes zero. Fix by recomputing direction from each bootstrap block/trajectory with boundary handling, selecting blocks based on residual autocorrelation, and reporting that current evidence does not support predictive memory.

final:
## Research Trajectory

**Published context:** The identified source study reports spatial coarsening in this mechatronic metamaterial system. The supplied export is one 2,199-sample experimental aggregate, not 2,199 independent runs. The follow-up does not claim to rediscover coarsening or establish a new mechanism.

**Question and conditional hypothesis:** Does mean shear depend only on instantaneous correlation width, or does it also depend on the recent coarsening path? The proposal was that, at matched widths, shear might differ when width is growing versus shrinking. That would be consistent with lagged response or hysteresis, but could also reflect shared time trends, smoothing, or noise. The prediction was that lagged width change would improve held-out prediction and that a growth-versus-decline contrast would remain directionally stable after accounting for time and serial dependence. Neither outcome is proof of a mechanism.

**Observed data and analysis trajectory:** The supplied measurements had 2,199 rows, no missing required values or duplicate timestamps, and highly regular 0.003333-second spacing. Width ranged from 0 to 17.1456; shear ranged from 0.04599 to 0.21571. Their descriptive Pearson correlation was 0.5492. The first analysis reported a small lag-model improvement, but its matched-width contrast and bootstrap were judged invalid: the contrast pooled across time, and bootstrap indexing broke the intended contiguous resampling. A subsequent attempt failed because the time-only model requested a nonexistent feature column. After that was fixed, the lagged model performed slightly worse than the width-plus-time baseline. A later contrast and bootstrap were again judged mismatched to the intended estimand.

The final reported analysis used actual elapsed-time lag differences and recomputed the matched growth-versus-decline contrast in contiguous-block bootstrap replicates. Blocked expanding-window results were: time-only RMSE 0.01038949, MAE 0.007651518; width-plus-time RMSE 0.009663956, MAE 0.007268262; and the 0.10-second lag-augmented model RMSE 0.009677134, MAE 0.007350481. Lag sensitivities were worse at 0.05 seconds (RMSE 0.01053883, MAE 0.008081386) and substantially worse at 0.20 seconds (RMSE 0.02332396, MAE 0.01407957). The final matched-width support was 1.5746–13.4715, with 986 growing and 756 shrinking samples. The smoothed growth-minus-decline shear contrast was -0.003122128; its reported 95% block-bootstrap interval was -0.004902243 to 0.002571514, spanning zero.

**Interpretation and open alternatives:** These results do not support the proposed predictive-memory pattern in this export: the primary lag model did not improve on width plus time, and the final directional contrast was uncertain. Residual lag-1 autocorrelation remained high (0.8652), so substantial temporal structure was unmodeled. Expanding-window validation tests later periods and may confound prediction with regime changes. The bootstrap interval is descriptive for this single aggregate, not independent-run inference; its 30-sample blocks may not capture the dependence indicated by residual autocorrelation, and direction labels were not recomputed from each resampled trajectory. Accordingly, neither the score differences nor the contrast establish absence or presence of physical memory. Shared temporal trends, export aggregation or smoothing, measurement noise, and insufficiently representative block uncertainty remain alternatives. Repeated runs, raw image sequences, and documented uncertainty would be needed for stronger tests; novelty beyond the supplied source context remains unresolved.
